label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",
   "what": "Retail load obligation: short 140 MW x (load / normal load) in N.Y.C. at fixed price R = 45.65, hedged by a long WEST position at H = 34.05, 24 h; P&L = (R - N.Y.C. price) + (WEST price - H), times load"
  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: A January arctic outflow lifts N.Y.C. load about 10% above a typical winter day, pushing the daily peak toward the Elliott-era range. Constrained upstate-to-downstate transfers and limited import capability widen the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $200/MWh on each of 10 shocked days, because the pocket clears on local gas-fired and import-limited supply. The short 140 MW retail load obligation (P5) bears the full spread loss, while the 24-hour long spread (P2) recovers only a small part. Gas and WEST on-peak prices are left unshocked to isolate the congestion channel. The engine sensitivity implies a net loss of roughly $6.1M over 10 days, and the 200 $/MWh spread lies below the winter implausibility bound of 503.7.

A short, sharp cold snap pushes N.Y.C. into a severe local shortage, widening the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $320/MWh over 5 days, while real-time upstate prices settle 40% below day-ahead as the day-ahead market over-commits WEST supply. The spread shock dominates the loss through the 140 MW retail obligation (P5). The DART move hurts the long WEST swap (P1) and the heat-rate call (P4), while the short-real-time premium gain on P3 offsets only part of it. The WEST on-peak price is cut 40% against the unshocked path, which removes some of P1 and P4 value. The combined engine-style estimate is roughly $5.3M, with low precision because the sensitivities are not additive.

A prolonged cold snap of 15 days raises N.Y.C. load about 15% above normal, widening the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $120/MWh on each day as import corridors saturate. Henry Hub gas rises 15% on the same days, which modestly helps the long WEST positions (P1 and P4), while a $10/MMBtu gas basis at N.Y.C. delivery cuts the heat-rate call payoff (P4) without moving power prices. Real-time WEST clears 20% below day-ahead, a small drag on P1 and P4. Engine-style estimate: about $5.7M net over 15 days, dominated by the sustained spread on P5, with P4 losses capped at its base payoff.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A severe January cold front pushes N.Y.C. load about 20% above a typical winter day while import corridors from upstate and Canada saturate. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $240/MWh on each of 7 shocked days, close to the Winter Storm Elliott real-time spread of $338.5/MWh but kept below it for plausibility. The short 140 MW retail obligation (P5) absorbs most of the loss, partly offset by the 24-hour long spread (P2). WEST on-peak prices, gas, and DART are left unshocked to isolate the zone-volume channel. The engine sensitivities imply roughly $5.4M net loss over the 7 days, and the 240 $/MWh spread and 1.20 load ratio sit inside the winter implausibility ceilings.

A prolonged winter pattern keeps the Hudson Valley and N.Y.C. pocket tight for 20 consecutive days. Load stays at normal levels, so the driver is persistent congestion rather than peak load. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $80/MWh every day, which steadily erodes the value of the short 140 MW retail obligation (P5). Real-time prices clear 50% above day-ahead on the same days as the day-ahead market under-commits imports, which hurts the DART position (P3). The long 24-hour spread (P2) recovers part of the spread loss. Engine-style sensitivities imply roughly $5.6M net loss over the 20 days, with low precision because the channels are not additive.

A cold snap with heavy heating demand lifts N.Y.C. load about 25% above normal on 12 days, as the Elliott-style real-time spike pattern reappears in both the pocket and upstate. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh, the main loss driver through the 140 MW retail obligation (P5). Real-time clears 80% above day-ahead on the same days, which hits the day-ahead minus real-time receivable on 50 MW (P3). The long 24-hour spread (P2) provides a partial offset. Gas and WEST on-peak prices are not shocked, so the long WEST swap (P1) and heat-rate call (P4) contribute little. Engine-style estimate is about $6.3M net over 12 days, with low confidence because the DART and zone channels interact.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A cold front lifts N.Y.C. load about 20% above a typical winter day while upstate WEST on-peak prices fall 25% against the unshocked path, as surplus upstate hydro and wind keep WEST cheap. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $190/MWh on each of 9 shocked days because the pocket clears on import-limited local supply. The short 140 MW retail obligation (P5) absorbs most of the loss. The 24-hour long spread (P2) offsets part of it. The WEST decline cuts value from the long WEST swap (P1) and heat-rate call (P4). Gas and DART are unshocked to isolate the system and zone channels. Engine-style sensitivities imply a net loss of roughly $5.6M over 9 days, with low precision because the channels are not additive.

A two-week winter blocking pattern keeps Hudson Valley and N.Y.C. transfers constrained while load runs about 15% above normal. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $125/MWh every day for 14 consecutive days, so the loss builds slowly rather than through a single spike. The short 140 MW retail obligation (P5) bears the cumulative spread loss, and the 24-hour long spread (P2) recovers only part of it. Gas, WEST on-peak prices, and DART are left at the unshocked path, so the scenario tests persistence in the congestion channel alone. Because the duration is long relative to the other scenarios, the net loss is driven by accumulated days rather than peak magnitude. Engine-style estimate is roughly $5.3M net over 14 days, with low confidence on the cumulative sum.

A short, intense cold snap drives N.Y.C. load about 10% above normal and pushes the pocket spread out by $250/MWh on each of 6 days, as local units and imports are unable to meet evening demand. Real-time WEST clears 250% above day-ahead on the same days, which is the opposite direction from the earlier DART scenarios and hits the day-ahead minus real-time receivable on 50 MW (P3) directly. The spread loss on the short 140 MW retail obligation (P5) dominates, partly offset by the 24-hour long spread (P2). WEST on-peak prices and gas are unshocked, so the long WEST swap (P1) and heat-rate call (P4) contribute little. Engine-style sensitivities imply a net loss of roughly $5.4M over 6 days, with moderate confidence in the spread component.

2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).

scenario.narrative: A heat wave pushes N.Y.C. load to about 5% above a typical summer day while upstate supply stays available, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $220/MWh for 10 days. The load ratio of 1.05 is a moderate heat-driven increase, and the spread widening reflects the constrained import capability into the pocket. P5 is short N.Y.C. retail load and loses on the widened spread, while P2 gains only part of the offset. WEST on-peak, gas, and real-time-to-day-ahead gaps are held at neutral so the loss isolates the congestion channel. Engine sensitivity gives about 645k loss per 50 $/MWh over 5 days, so 220 $/MWh over 10 days is about 5.7M gross, reduced slightly by the load gain.

A prolonged heat wave keeps N.Y.C. load only slightly above normal (ratio 1.02) for 30 days while transmission into the pocket stays constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is 70 $/MWh wider on every shocked day. The loss is a slow bleed on the retail load obligation P5 that is only partly offset by the congestion position P2. WEST on-peak prices, gas, and the day-ahead to real-time gap are unchanged, so no offsetting gains from P1 or P4 are assumed. Engine sensitivity of about 645k per 50 $/MWh over 5 days scales to roughly 5.4M over 30 days, and the small load effect is treated as negligible. The cumulative duration is the main driver of this case.

scenario.narrative: A heat wave forecast is overstated: day-ahead prices embed a hotter load path than materializes, so real-time clears 40% below day-ahead on the shocked days and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 100 $/MWh for 20 days. Load ratio is held at 1.00, meaning the realized peak is near normal rather than extra hot. The dart move hurts the book through the engine-sensitivity channel that links the day-ahead to real-time gap to P1 and P4, while the spread widening drives the loss on P5 net of P2. Engine sensitivity suggests about 173k per 5 days for the dart move and 1.29M per 5 days for the spread, giving roughly 5.8M over 20 days. The dart sign is taken from the engine and is the least certain element.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A heat wave pushes N.Y.C. load up about 4% above a typical summer day while upstate supply remains ample, so transmission into the pocket is constrained and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $280/MWh for 7 days. The spread is held just under the historical maximum of 289.7 $/MWh for summer. The loss sits mainly on P5, the short N.Y.C. retail obligation hedged only at WEST, and P2 offsets part of it. WEST on-peak, gas, and the day-ahead to real-time gap are held neutral so the result isolates the congestion channel. Engine sensitivities imply roughly 3,550 $/MWh-day of loss on P5 and about 600 $/MWh-day of gain on P2, which gives a net loss near 5.7M over 7 days.

A heat wave in the pocket coincides with an upstate price decline. Upstate supply is ample and congestion into N.Y.C. persists, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $130/MWh over 15 days. WEST on-peak prices fall 15% relative to the unshocked path, and real-time clears 20% below day-ahead on the shocked days. The WEST fall hurts the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, and the real-time discount adds to the damage. P3 gains on the lower real-time price, which partly offsets the loss. Load is raised only 3% so the scenario does not rely on load. The engine sensitivity to the day-ahead to real-time gap is the least certain element.

A long, moderate heat wave keeps N.Y.C. load about 20% above a typical summer day for 25 days, and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $80/MWh on every shocked day. Sustained high pocket load keeps the import corridor saturated, so the spread widening persists rather than spiking. The loss is a slow bleed on P5 that P2 only partly offsets. WEST on-peak prices, gas, and the day-ahead to real-time gap stay at neutral, so the result comes from duration and load rather than from price spikes or gas. The load effect on P5 is small in the engine sensitivities, so the spread drives most of the loss. Confidence is low because no analogue spans a 25-day sustained pocket widening.

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A two-week heat wave lifts N.Y.C. load to about 10% above a typical summer day, and import corridors into the pocket stay saturated, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh on each of 14 days. Upstate gas prices fall 20% on the same days as cheap regional supply weakens the WEST heat-rate link. The main loss comes from P5, the short N.Y.C. retail obligation hedged only at WEST, and P2 offsets part of it. The gas drop reduces the heat-rate call P4 and the spread-driven P5 loss sits well inside the summer historical range. WEST on-peak prices and the day-ahead to real-time gap are held neutral so the result isolates spread, load, and gas. Engine sensitivities imply roughly 2,590 $/MWh-day of net loss from the spread, so 2,100 $/MWh-days gives about 5.4M, plus load and gas effects.

scenario.narrative: A short but intense heat wave pushes N.Y.C. load about 6% above normal while upstate transmission is fully committed, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $335/MWh over 6 days. This sits just below the summer implausibility ceiling of 363.1 $/MWh and within the historical maximum range of about 290 $/MWh once the ceiling is considered. The loss lands mainly on P5, and P2 offsets only a fraction because its spread strike sits far below the shock. WEST on-peak prices, gas, and the day-ahead to real-time gap are held neutral so the loss is attributable to the congestion channel alone. Engine sensitivity implies about 2,590 $/MWh-day of net loss, giving roughly 5.2M over 6 days, with the small load effect adding a little more.

A heat wave pushes N.Y.C. load up about 2% while upstate prices slump: WEST on-peak falls 30% relative to the unshocked path and gas falls 25% on the same days, so the upstate supply glut coincides with a pocket that stays short. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $200/MWh over 10 days because transmission into the pocket is constrained. The WEST price fall hurts the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 through both the on-peak level and the gas link, and the wider spread hurts P5 net of the P2 offset. Load is kept modest so the scenario does not depend on load. Engine sensitivities imply roughly 2,590 $/MWh-day from the spread, about 2,000 $/MWh-days total, plus the WEST and gas losses.

2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.

4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A moderate large-load shortfall of about 900 MW (load_peak_ratio 0.97, large_load_shock_mw -900) reduces summer peak load, but the main loss channel is congestion. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh for 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd +70), which is inside the summer implausible ceiling of 363.1 and below the historical maximum of 289.7 for this factor. This requires a concurrent Zone J import or transmission derate that the load shortfall does not itself imply, so the physical coherence is weak. Small WEST declines (ref_onpeak_pct -5) and the load reduction add minor losses. The engine-linear estimate is about $5.75M, which is unverified.

Slower large-load arrivals of about 1,400 MW (large_load_shock_mw -1400, load_peak_ratio 0.96) coincide with a concentrated 10-day Zone J congestion event. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $200/MWh for 10 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd +200), which is above the historical summer maximum of 289.7 but below the implausible ceiling of 363.1. The mechanism is a Zone J import limit or peaker-retention constraint that keeps N.Y.C. prices high while WEST softens modestly (ref_onpeak_pct -20). Real-time and gas are held flat in this case, so the loss comes almost entirely from the short P5 retail exposure. The engine-linear estimate is about $5.47M, which is unverified.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.

1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large new loads arrive about 700 MW slower than forecast, trimming the summer daily peak to 0.98 of normal (large_load_shock_mw -700, load_peak_ratio 0.98). Real-time clears 15% above day-ahead (dart_pct +15) as the day-ahead commitment undershoots the realised evening peak, which hurts the day-ahead-short-real-time-long P3 position. A Zone J transmission or retained-peaker constraint widens N.Y.C. minus WEST by $100/MWh for 20 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd +100), which is inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7 for this factor. WEST on-peak falls 15% (ref_onpeak_pct -15) and Henry Hub falls 20% (gas_hh_pct -20), lowering P1 and P4. The main loss is the short retail obligation P5, partly offset by the congestion-long P2. The engine-linear estimate is about $5.4M, which is unverified and assumes the Zone J constraint is not already priced in.

Large-load arrivals run about 1,500 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -1500), and the summer daily peak falls to 0.95 of normal (load_peak_ratio 0.95). Upstate oversupply collapses WEST on-peak prices by 90% (ref_onpeak_pct -90), close to the summer implausible-below ceiling of -90.8. Henry Hub falls 50% (gas_hh_pct -50), reducing the heat-rate call P4 on top of the long WEST swap P1. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens only modestly, by $25/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +25), so the retail short P5 contributes a smaller share than in the congestion cases. Day-ahead and real-time remain at parity (dart_pct 0). The loss is driven mainly by P1 and P4, with P5 a secondary contributor. The engine-linear estimate is about $5.6M, which is unverified.

A 10-day burst of slower large-load arrivals (large_load_shock_mw -1400, load_peak_ratio 0.96) combines a real-time premium with a sharp Zone J congestion widening. Real-time clears 120% above day-ahead (dart_pct +120), which is inside the summer implausible-above ceiling of 284.7 but above the historical maximum of 207.8, so it is treated as a stressed case. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $180/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +180) for the same 10 days, below the implausible ceiling of 363.1. WEST on-peak falls 20% (ref_onpeak_pct -20) and gas is held flat, so the loss comes mainly from the short retail P5 and the real-time exposure of P3. P2 offsets part of the loss. The engine-linear estimate is about $5.2M, which is unverified and requires the real-time spike and congestion widening to co-occur.
